newsitem.title: USA: US communities press for brownfields legislation.
newsitem.headline: US communities press for brownfields legislation.

text.p: Local U.S. communities Friday urged the federal government to pass legislation that would encourage redevelopment of abandoned, polluted industrial and commercial sites.
Developers often do not want to touch the so-called brownfield properties because of the potential liability they could face for contamination caused by previous owners.

The National Association of Local Government Environmental Professionals urged Congress to put into law policies that the Clinton administration had adopted to ensure that prospective buyers were not held liable for waste left by former owners.

"NALGEP calls upon the federal government to work with local officials to create the liability tools, and funding and other partnership incentives that will achieve long-term renewal in our communities," David Padgett, environmental affairs manager for Colorado Springs, said in a statement.
The group said legislation should provide tax credits or deductions for expenses linked to assessing and cleaning brownfields sites, and tax breaks for redeveloping them.
It also called for Congress to expand authority under the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act to allow transportation funding to be used to redevelop brownfields.
Democrats and Republicans have introduced legislation in the Senate seeking to provide states with grants to assess brownfield sites and low interest loans for cleanups.
The bills would also relieve buyers from cleanup liability if they did not cause the problem or took steps to limit it.

In a report released Friday, the local environmental officials said a brownfields law should clearly distinguish between the worst toxic waste sites, which qualify for Superfund cleanups, and less contaminated sites.

They said legislation should also give the Environmental Protection Agency authority to let states set liability limits and set cleanup standards for less contaminated sites, as long as a state meets minimum requirements to protect public health and the environment.
